_README: Every human judgement about this ROM lives in this file; the
generated listings are disposable, so renaming is free.
What to do next, roughly in order:
Read the coverage it reports. Low coverage is normal at
first and is the number you are trying to move.
2. Every unresolved indirect jump it reports is a hole. Add the
target to `entries`, or the pointer pair to `ram_vectors` if
the handler is installed into RAM.
Finds the sound code and the tables feeding it.
4. Name things in `labels` as soon as you know what they are.
See docs/method.md for the working order and docs/pitfalls.md for
the traps that each cost real time.

comments.rom:DE5C: CONFIRMED LIVE -- first live-verified finding for this project. The score-award routine, found by grepping for SED (2 sites in this ROM, the same short-candidate-list technique the sibling projects used). Takes an award-type index in X and adds a packed-BCD value into the current player's score: CurrentPlayer (ram_007A) is shifted left twice to give a 4-byte stride, so player 0's score is ram_0046-ram_0049 and player 1's is ram_004A-ram_004D, most-significant byte first (8 BCD digits each). dat_FEDC supplies the low digit pair and dat_FEE4 the high pair. Decoded, the 8-entry table is: 0=100, 1=50, 2=20, 3=500, 4=1000, 5=200, 6 and 7 unused (zero) -- matching the manual's table exactly across all six documented awards (large asteroid 20, medium 50, small 100, large saucer 200, small saucer 1,000, other player's ship 500). NOTE a real divergence from the sibling projects: these values are stored at FACE VALUE, not at the x10 BCD scale independently found in both Galaga and Ms. Pac-Man. BCD $0100 here means 100 points, not 1,000. Assuming the family convention would have mis-scaled every award by a factor of ten. LIVE-VERIFIED against run-01.inp (tools/probe-score.lua), watching both players' score bytes across the whole recording: every positive delta was exactly a manual value -- +20 x23, +50 x40, +100 x66, +200 x3 -- with no unexplained amounts. The 500 and 1,000 entries are read from the table only; neither a small saucer nor a player-versus-player kill occurred in this recording, so those two are NOT yet live-confirmed.
comments.rom:DE75: The bonus-ship award, and the mechanism behind the shared TEAM score -- confirmed live, and prompted by the user's observation that Team mode shows a shared score at top-centre. The BCD add above carries out of ram_0048/ram_0049 (the low four digits) exactly when the score crosses a 10,000 boundary, matching the manual's 'bonus ship every 10,000 points'; the award path then increments ReserveShips (ram_0052, newly named -- a per-slot array indexed by CurrentPlayer). The gate here is the interesting part: if GameMode (ram_0082) is 1 AND CurrentPlayer is not 2, the award is skipped. CurrentPlayer therefore has a THIRD value beyond the two players, and since the score routine strides by CurrentPlayer*4, slot 2's score occupies ram_004E-ram_0051 -- ScoreTeam (newly named). LIVE-VERIFIED against run-01.inp (tools/probe-team.lua), which contains one-player, team and competitive segments: GameMode reads $FF in the one-player segment, 1 during team play and 2 during competitive play. During the team segment ScoreTeam is exactly the sum of the two individual scores, checked at two independent moments (70+20=90, and 440+370=810), while in the one-player and competitive segments it stays 0. ReserveShips for slot 2 was also seen depleting (4 down to 0) only during team play, matching the manual's 'sharing reserve ships'. So team mode keeps both individual scores AND a shared total, and routes the bonus ship to the shared pool.
comments.rom:D66A: The controller read, and the key to the user's hyperspace report. This handles a two-button ProLine pad: INPT1,Y and INPT0,Y are read, inverted, and stored per player into Button1 (ram_00B8,X) and Button2 (ram_00BA,X), X being the player index. Measured across run-01.inp, Button1 is pressed 503 times by player 1 versus 46 for Button2 -- the signature of fire versus a situational action -- and Button2 is the one rom:D358 tests before calling rom:sub_D540.
comments.rom:D540: HYPERSPACE (the user's 'emergency teleport'), reached from rom:D358 when Button2 is pressed. Deliberately RATE-LIMITED: it returns immediately if ShipSpecialState (ram_007E,X) is already non-zero, so holding or mashing the button cannot re-trigger it while a jump is in progress. Measured in run-01.inp: 73 Button2 presses produced only 12 actual jumps, which matches the user's description of spamming the button. On a real trigger it sets ShipSpecialState to 2 and ShipPhaseTimer (ram_0080,X) to $2C. That timer is counted DOWN at rom:D6BC, and the state machine at rom:L_D72E tests it against $29 -- three steps below the starting value -- which is therefore the hyperspace RE-ENTRY checkpoint, where ram_00A5 is consulted (rom:L_D79E) to decide whether re-entry is survivable. The other two checkpoints it tests ($79, $51) are above $2C and so belong to other states, not to hyperspace.
comments.rom:D79E: The hyperspace RE-ENTRY check -- resolved with run-02, a recording the user made specifically to capture the effect (asteroids mostly cleared, teleport pressed repeatedly, deaths only from teleport). Confirmed by write-tapping ReserveShips: both deaths were written from PC=$D7BC, i.e. through THIS state-machine path and not any collision handler -- matching the user's 'no collision' report from the code side. A jump runs a three-phase sequence on ShipSpecialState (ram_007E) with ShipPhaseTimer (ram_0080) counting down one step per two frames: phase 2 (timer $2C, ship leaving), phase 3 (timer $DE, in hyperspace), then phase 1 (timer $2C again, re-entry). The check here fires when the timer reaches $29 DURING PHASE 1. TRAP, and the reason an earlier pass got this wrong: the timer passes through $29 in BOTH phase 2 and phase 1, six frames after the jump and again ~170 frames later. Only the phase-1 occurrence is the re-entry check; reading the phase-2 one produced a confident but meaningless measurement. RETRACTED with it: the earlier reading of ram_00A5 as the 'you die' flag. Across run-02 ram_00A5 is $FF at every single checkpoint, on surviving and fatal jumps alike, so it cannot be what decides. Measured: both fatal jumps died exactly 172 frames after the jump, while every survived jump completed its whole cycle in ~110 frames -- so what distinguishes them is that phase 3 ran LONG on the fatal ones. What ends phase 3 early (survival) versus letting it run on (death) is NOT yet established, and is the open question here.
comments.rom:D83D: HYPERSPACE RE-ENTRY -- and the answer to the user's report that the emergency teleport sometimes kills with no collision. It does, and by design. Two things happen here, and they are independent. FIRST, a landing spot is chosen at random: two calls to the PRNG (rom:sub_F8B2) produce an X and a Y (each halved and biased, giving a position inset from the screen edges), and rom:sub_F93C then tests that spot. If the test fails the routine does INC ram_0080,X, pushing the phase timer back up so the very next tick lands on $01 again and the whole draw repeats -- so the game RETRIES until it finds a clear spot. Materialising inside a rock is therefore explicitly prevented, and is NOT the cause of the deaths. SECOND, once a clear spot is found, rom:L_D85F draws ONE MORE random byte and compares it with #$32: if it is >= $32 the ship rematerialises normally (rom:L_D888 sets ShipSpecialState back to 0 and plays sound 3), and if it is < $32 the ship is destroyed (sound 5, then rom:sub_D87D sets ShipSpecialState to 3, the destruction sequence). That is a flat 50-in-256 chance -- about 19.5% -- of dying on every hyperspace re-entry, independent of the screen's contents. The manual documents hyperspace only as 'warp to a random location' and says nothing about the risk, so this is a genuine manual-versus-ROM divergence. Consistent with the user's observation across run-02: 7 jumps, 3 fatal (jumps 5, 6 and 7 all entered state 3, jumps 1-4 returned to state 0), and their own estimate of 'clearly less than 92% but higher than 0%'. 3-of-7 observed is above the 19.5% expectation but unremarkable at that sample size.
comments.rom:D818: The hyperspace phase-2 handler, dispatched from rom:L_D6BC. Phase 2 is the ship LEAVING: at timer $29 it blanks the ship's four object-array entries (rom:L_D823, making it vanish) and at timer $01 it runs the re-entry logic at rom:L_D83D. Correcting an earlier mis-mapping: phase 3 is NOT 'in hyperspace' as first assumed -- it is the DESTRUCTION sequence, only entered when the re-entry roll fails. A survived jump goes state 2 -> 0 and never touches phase 3 at all, which is exactly what run-02 shows for its four safe jumps.
comments.rom:D2B5: Wave spawn. Fills ObjType (ram_008C, newly named -- the per-object TYPE array, ~$2C slots, $FF meaning an empty slot) for indices 8 down to 0, and initialises a parallel per-object array at ram_1ACB from dat_FE45. The object system was decoded live rather than statically: see rom:sub_DCF4's comment for the asteroid size encoding and the split behaviour.
comments.rom:DCF4: CONFIRMED LIVE -- the asteroid size/split system, decoded by dumping the ObjType array either side of six scoring events in run-01 (tools/probe-rocks.lua) rather than by reading the collision code. Asteroid types are $32 large, $21 medium, $10 small, and the points are inverse to size exactly as the manual states: destroying $32 scores 20, $21 scores 50, $10 scores 100. Splitting is the classic cascade and was observed directly: a destroyed LARGE ($32) is replaced by TWO new MEDIUM ($21) slots; a destroyed MEDIUM by TWO new SMALL ($10) slots; a destroyed SMALL spawns nothing. Seen twice independently for large (frames 1414 and 1956), once for medium (1424) and twice for small (1476, 1570). Bit 7 of ObjType marks an object as destroyed/exploding rather than being a separate type: $10 becomes $90, $21 becomes $A1, $32 becomes $B2, and the player ship $23 becomes $A3 -- the same +$80 in every case, and the slot then clears to $FF a short time later. That also explains the ship value $A3 written by the hyperspace death path (see rom:D83D): it is simply the ship type with the exploding bit set. NOT yet confirmed: the identity of the other live types seen alongside these ($06 and $07, the latter occupying eight consecutive slots, which would fit a shot pool but is untested). SAUCER AND SHOT, added from the same technique on run-01's three +200 awards (tools/probe-ufo.lua). The saucer is ObjType $25 and it always occupies the SAME slot, index $19 -- a dedicated slot rather than one taken from the general pool -- and all three kills show that slot going $25 -> $A5. That is a fifth independent confirmation of the bit-7 destruction rule ($10/$90, $21/$A1, $32/$B2, $23/$A3, $25/$A5), which now holds for every object type observed destroyed. Across the whole recording $25 is present for about 994 frames, so the saucer is on screen only briefly. The manual's SMALL saucer (1,000 points) never appears in this recording -- no +1000 award occurs and no further saucer-like type is seen -- so its type byte is still unknown. Separately, the $06 objects are the PLAYER'S SHOTS: a $06 slot flips to $86 (destroyed) on the exact frame of every hit, seen for both asteroid kills and all three saucer kills, i.e. the shot is consumed on impact. The eight permanently-present $07 slots at $24-$2B are therefore NOT the shot pool as earlier guessed -- they are present for essentially the whole recording, so that guess is retracted and their identity is open. SMALL SAUCER, and a distinction the user's controlled run-03 isolated cleanly. The small saucer is ObjType $14 and it uses the SAME dedicated slot $19 as the large one, so that slot is simply 'the saucer' and the type byte distinguishes large ($25, 200 points) from small ($14, 1,000 points) -- both matching the manual. $14 -> $94 on destruction, a sixth confirmation of the bit-7 rule. run-03 contains two small saucers and the user deliberately let them die differently: the first (frames 5330-5392) flew into an asteroid and was destroyed with NO score award at all, while the second (5922-6142) was shot and awarded exactly +1000. So destruction and scoring are separate: the slot transitions to the exploding type either way, and the award is gated on the player having caused it. That also means an object-type transition alone is NOT evidence of a score event, which is worth remembering for any future probe built on this array. Observed progression in that recording, from a single run and so not a confirmed rule: four large saucers appear first (frames 2538-4808) and only then two small ones (5330 onward), consistent with small saucers arriving later, but no threshold has been measured. ARRAY BOUNDS, and a RETRACTION of the '$07 slots' from an earlier pass. Prompted by the user's point that if those slots were shots they should be consumed as shooting continues, the array's actual extent was measured: for every frame of a 4,599-frame window, indices $00-$23 (addresses $008C-$00AF) hold a valid object type, and indices $24 and beyond hold one on ZERO frames. So ObjType is exactly 36 slots, $008C-$00AF, and the 'eight permanently-present $07 objects' reported earlier were simply reads PAST THE END of the array into unrelated zero-page variables at $00B0-$00B7 that happen to contain $07. They were never objects, and the fact that some of them changed value was ordinary variable activity, not movement. Both the original shot-pool guess and its first retraction were reasoning about data that was not part of this array at all. This also positively identifies a byte left unexplained by the hyperspace work: ram_00A5 is $008C+$19, i.e. ObjType for the dedicated SAUCER slot (ObjTypeSaucer, newly named). The test at rom:D79E is reading whether a saucer is currently present ($FF = none, and negative), not consulting a 'death flag' -- which is why it read $FF throughout run-02, a recording with no saucers in it. The hyperspace conclusion itself is unaffected: the ~19.5% re-entry roll was traced through rom:L_D83D/rom:L_D85F and never depended on ram_00A5.
comments.rom:D284: The difficulty selector, confirming the manual's four levels from the ROM. Difficulty (ram_0083, newly named) is incremented with a clamp at 3 here and decremented with a floor at 0 at rom:L_D28E, so its range is 0-3 -- Novice, Intermediate, Advanced, Expert. Measured across the recordings: run-01, run-02 and run-03 all ran at 1, and run-04 -- which the user recorded specifically on Expert -- reads 3, confirming the mapping's top end. Cross-check on the bottom end: the manual says Novice has no saucers, and all three difficulty-1 recordings do contain saucers, so 1 cannot be Novice. rom:D123 separately adds Difficulty to a base index of $0A before a display call, consistent with selecting one of four level-name strings.
comments.rom:F51B: CONFIRMS THE MANUAL FROM THE ROM: 'Novice features no saucers'. The saucer routine (rom:sub_F510) loads Difficulty and returns immediately if it is zero, so on Novice no saucer is ever processed at all.
comments.rom:F45A: The per-difficulty parameter lookup, and the mechanism behind the user's observation that saucers arrive faster on Expert. Difficulty indexes dat_F4B1, a 4-byte table reading $40, $60, $80, $DF for levels 0-3, and the result is stored in DifficultyCap (ram_0084, newly named). rom:sub_F89E then accumulates into SaucerPressure (ram_0089, newly named, one per player) and CLAMPS it to DifficultyCap -- so a harder setting simply permits a larger value. SaucerPressure is consumed at rom:F7F9, which copies it and its halved value into ram_1A90/ram_1A91 and then checks ObjTypeSaucer for $FF (no saucer currently present) before proceeding -- i.e. it feeds the saucer spawn path. Higher difficulty therefore raises the ceiling on this value and saucers come sooner, which is what the recordings show: measured live, the first saucer appears at frame 1070 in the Expert run versus frame 2006 in an otherwise comparable difficulty-1 run, and the small saucer ($14) arrives as the THIRD saucer on Expert (frame 2522) rather than the fifth (frame 5330) at difficulty 1. NOT established: the precise units of SaucerPressure, and whether the large-versus-small saucer choice is driven by this same value or by a separate rule.
comments.rom:DD15: THE SPLIT LOGIC, and the third thing Difficulty controls -- the manual's 'simplified asteroid splitting' for Novice, confirmed from the ROM. The fragment type is computed arithmetically: destroyed type MINUS $91. That matches every size observed live: destroyed large $B2-$91 = $21 (medium), destroyed medium $A1-$91 = $10 (small), and destroyed small $90-$91 goes negative, caught by the BMI, so a small asteroid produces nothing. rom:sub_DD3D is the fragment spawner: it scans slots $17 down to 0 for a free one ($FF) and copies the parent's position and velocity arrays into it, returning without doing anything if the array is full. Difficulty then selects how many times it is called: Novice (0) branches to rom:L_DD37 and gets ONE call; Intermediate and Advanced (1, 2) fall to rom:L_DD34 and get TWO; Expert (3) additionally tests ram_0040 AND #$03 -- a 1-in-4 draw off the PRNG's own index -- and on a hit makes an EXTRA call before those two, so up to THREE fragments. LIVE-CONFIRMED by counting the net change in live asteroid slots per destruction: in the difficulty-1 run every one of 18 splits netted +1 (one destroyed, two created), while the Expert run showed +1 eighteen times AND +2 twice -- three fragments from one rock. It also showed +0 twice, consistent with sub_DD3D finding no free slot. That slot exhaustion, plus the small sample, explains why the observed extra-fragment rate (2 of 22) sits below the nominal 1-in-4. The Novice single-fragment case is code-derived only -- no recording at difficulty 0 exists to test it.
comments.rom:DD3D: The fragment spawner. Scans ObjType slots $17 down to 0 for a free one ($FF) and, on finding it, copies the parent object's position and velocity arrays (ram_18EC, ram_18A4, ram_190D, ram_18C8, ram_1972) across. If no slot is free it returns having done nothing, which is why some Expert splits were observed producing fewer fragments than the branch count at rom:L_DD15 would predict.

blocks.name: dat_E000
blocks.note: Day one. CONFIRMED free of missed code: every JSR/JMP byte pattern in the ROM that appeared to target inside a gap was re-checked against the addresses the disassembler actually reached as code, and all of them turned out to be byte patterns sitting inside data rather than real calls -- so no traced code branches into this range. Declared as a data block to close the gap; contents not yet characterised. The largest gap, and dominated by $00 (2,236 of 4,446 bytes) with $FF next -- sparse rather than dense, which fits bitmap/sprite data with a lot of empty space, but that is a signature guess, not a finding.

blocks.name: dat_C000
blocks.note: Day one. CONFIRMED free of missed code: every JSR/JMP byte pattern in the ROM that appeared to target inside a gap was re-checked against the addresses the disassembler actually reached as code, and all of them turned out to be byte patterns sitting inside data rather than real calls -- so no traced code branches into this range. Declared as a data block to close the gap; contents not yet characterised. Sits at the very base of the mapped window, page-aligned and ending exactly where RESET begins -- the same structural position the sibling Ms. Pac-Man project's character set occupies, so a font/tile set is the first hypothesis to test. It is NOT a padded glyph grid of the kind found there: a phase scan for a per-glyph pad byte across cell sizes 3-16 shows no clear winner (best spread 14 points at cell 16, versus a ~25-point spread with an unambiguous phase in the confirmed case). So either the cells carry no padding, or this is not a glyph grid at all. Untested, deliberately: nothing here is asserted yet.

blocks.name: dat_FDCE
blocks.note: Day one. CONFIRMED free of missed code: every JSR/JMP byte pattern in the ROM that appeared to target inside a gap was re-checked against the addresses the disassembler actually reached as code, and all of them turned out to be byte patterns sitting inside data rather than real calls -- so no traced code branches into this range. Declared as a data block to close the gap; contents not yet characterised. Runs to the ROM's top and contains the hardware vectors at $FFFA-$FFFF (NMI $D2FC, RESET $D000, IRQ $D32B), which is why it shows as a gap in every project -- vector bytes are data, not executed code. Declared with an explicit length rather than an end address, because the tool's `end` is exclusive and $FFFF would otherwise be left unclaimed. PARTIALLY IDENTIFIED: contains the score-award point tables at $FEDC (low BCD pair) and $FEE4 (high BCD pair), 8 entries each -- see rom:DE5C. The rest of the block is still uncharacterised.

notes.rom:
Asteroids (NTSC) (Atari) (1987) (DFB93F40).a78
mapper linear, 16 KB, NTSC
no POKEY declared; audio is the TIA's two voices

Vectors: IRQ $D32B  NMI $D2FC  RESET $D000

Written by init.py. Everything here is read from the cartridge; the
judgement calls are yours to add.
